mlb.headline: Led by King's all-in relief effort, Padres fight and force Game 4
mlb.body:
SAN DIEGO -- Didn’t matter how. The Padres only needed to find a way. They trailed two games to none and faced elimination on Tuesday night in this instant classic of a National League Division Series against Milwaukee. They had no Mason Miller and no Adrian Morejon at the back end of their bullpen. They found themselves on the ropes again and again in a Game 3 that swung back and forth deep into the San Diego night.

But when the dust had settled … when Xander Bogaerts had scooped Christian Yelich’s one-hop line drive, stepped on second, then fired to first … when the 45,000-plus who packed Petco Park long before first pitch could finally, mercifully exhale … the Padres had done exactly that.  Somehow, they had found a way. Ace Michael King -- two days after he’d pitched five innings in Game 2 -- nailed down the last six outs of San Diego’s breathless 4-3 Game 3 victory over Milwaukee. His 40th pitch was a slider that Christian Yelich lined 107 mph at Bogaerts, who started a game-ending double play that sent Petco Park into a frenzy. Amid the delirium, King stood stationary on the mound and slowly broke into a smile. It had been more than four years since he last recorded a save. But if there was ever a time, this was it. “I have bullets in my arm that I don't want to save,” King said afterward. “You're in an elimination game, you want everybody to be all-in on it. Not just me included. We have a bunch of dogs down there that are all-in.”

Elimination game? The Padres have another one Wednesday night now, too. The Brewers lead the series, 2-1, with Game 4 set for Wednesday at 7 p.m. PT. If the first three games are any indication, expect plenty of drama. All three have been decided by a single run, the first time a postseason series has begun with three one-run games since the 2021 NLCS between the Dodgers and Braves. “Finally were able to come out on the right end of things in this one,” said manager Craig Stammen.  And they did it without their two best relief weapons. A few hours before first pitch on Tuesday, Miller called the Padres. His wife had gone into labor. He would not be available for Game 3 and was subsequently placed on the paternity list. His absence would make things tricky, but the Padres had long been planning for this eventuality.  And, on paper at least, they had another elite relief weapon to cover that closer role. Or so we all thought.  Unbeknownst to the public -- and to the Brewers -- Morejon had been dealing with fatigue in his left shoulder. “Stickiness,” Stammen called it. Morejon played catch before the game. He even threw off the bullpen mound. But the Padres weren’t going to push it. “It was hard to map out from the beginning,” Stammen said. “Just because both of those guys are unavailable, and we'd relied on them so much throughout the year. It was a chance for the other guys to pick those two up.”

Nothing, it seems, will come easy in this series, and why should it? These are the 103-win Brewers, owners of baseball’s best record. If the Padres are going to pull off the remarkable comeback they believe they’re capable of, it’s going to take a herculean effort. Clearly. The task is only one-third finished, and consider what the Padres expended to even get here. “At the end of the day, it was win or go home, right?” said Manny Machado. “Back up against the wall. We had nothing to lose but go out there and play our baseball like we’ve been doing all year.”  For the third straight game, San Diego grabbed an early two-run lead. For the third straight game, Milwaukee erased that deficit. Jake Cronenworth’s solo homer -- left-on-left against Brewers reliever JoJo Romero -- put the Padres in front for good. The ending was anything but straightforward. Bogaerts’ baserunning savvy created the fourth run. In one leaping motion, he evaded Miguel Andujar’s ground ball and broken bat on his way to third base. When Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt threw the ball away, Bogaerts raced home and slid in safely. Milwaukee clawed one back, but Bradgley Rodriguez escaped the seventh inning with the lead intact. And that’s when it became clear: This wasn’t going to be the ending anyone had envisioned. King spent the seventh inning pacing in the bullpen. Eventually the phone rang. He hadn’t pitched in relief since Game 3 of last year’s Wild Card Series. But that was different. King did not pitch in that series otherwise. In this instance, he’d thrown 72 pitches *two days ago*.  “He came in the office today and said I'm available,” Stammen said.

“I knew that there was a chance it was going to be late in the game because of Mason's wife,” King said. “But six outs to end the game is six outs to end the game. I wasn't as crisp as I'd like to be.  “But I'm very happy for a Game 4.” (Yes, he wants to pitch in that one, too.) It wasn’t clear that Morejon was unavailable until King sat down in the dugout following his scoreless eighth. Where you’d expect action in the Padres bullpen, there was none. This would be King’s game to win or lose. “It's all hands on deck,” said Cronenworth. “He went out there and picked us up big time.” King became the 16th pitcher to throw five innings as a starter and record a save in the same playoff series since saves became an official stat in 1969. He’s the first since current teammate Walker Buehler in the 2024 World Series. Fittingly, with their season on the line once again, the Padres will hand the ball to Buehler in Game 4. Their plans beyond Buehler remain unclear. Those are largely contingent upon the availability of Miller and/or Morejon. The Padres just don’t know. But their objective is the same as it was on Tuesday night:  Find a way.

mlb.headline: Rays sweep their way past Yankees to reach 3rd ALCS in franchise history
mlb.body:
NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, Kevin Cash set the tone for the rowdy celebration raging in the visitors' clubhouse at Yankee Stadium with a message that made it clear the Rays weren’t done. They had accomplished their regular-season goals, getting back to the postseason and winning their first American League East title in five years, but that wasn’t the end. They had more in mind. Eleven more wins. Three more chances to pop champagne, pour out bottles of beer, smoke cigars, sing and dance together.

The Rays took another big step toward their ultimate goal on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, capping a sweep of the Yankees with a 4-3 victory in Game 3 of the AL Division Series, then once again turned the clubhouse at Yankee Stadium into their bar, lounge and dance floor.

Three wins down, eight more to go.

“We're loving it, man. We want to keep going,” a shirtless and soaked Nick Martinez said amid the celebration. “Like Cashy said, there's two more bites on the bone for us, and we know it. We know what's at stake. We know we want to keep playing.”​

Game 1 of the AL Championship Series is set for Monday at Tropicana Field, with the Rays hosting the winner of the Guardians-White Sox series that Chicago currently leads, 2-1. The Rays earned their spot by completing the first sweep in a best-of-five postseason series (or longer) in franchise history, and they dealt the Yankees only their second sweep (alongside the 1980 ALCS) in a best-of-five series. “Very special. Not an easy feat,” Martinez said. “Again, \[the Yankees are\] a very dangerous team. It's great to not have to play another game because you don't want to leave a team like that hanging around.”

Recognizing the work ahead of them, the Rays made sure they savored the moment.  A year to the day after their ownership group’s introductory press conference at George M. Steinbrenner Field, Rays managing partner Patrick Zalupski, co-chair Bill Cosgrove and CEO Ken Babby stood on the edge of the fray and smiled. Nearly the entire roster took part in a choreographed dance in the clubhouse. Players sang and danced to Jay-Z’s “Empire State of Mind” and Frank Sinatra’s “Theme from New York, New York” rang through the sound system. “I love drinking beer, and I love popping bottles. That's what it comes down to. I love it,” outfielder Ryan Vilade said. “This team is so special. We play for one another. We love each other, and we're not done. We don't want it to end.” When Cash made his way through the stadium’s lower-level tunnel and sat behind a table for his postgame press conference, he looked shockingly dry considering the state of the group he’d just walked away from. There was a reason for that. “This is my second shirt, second hat,” he quipped. “I've changed it twice.”

None of this was expected of the Rays. They were widely picked to finish last in the AL East. Even as they spent much of the season atop the AL standings, observers singled out other contenders as the league’s “team to beat.” But they proved themselves throughout the 162-game marathon, and they handily beat the AL’s second-best team in a three-game sprint by playing their game. They pitched well. They played clean defense. And their dynamic lineup showed it can score in a bunch of different ways. “They're a team by every definition. Every sense of the word 'team,' it's there. I've never seen anything like it,” president of baseball operations Erik Neander said. “These guys care so much for one another, and you want to win for so many reasons: the community, the team, it's our job. But man, for this group, you want them to do it that much more.  “You want to see them have these moments because of the way they've come together, and they deserve it.” As they did in the first two games at Tropicana Field, the Rays rode their starting pitchers most of the way in Game 3. Martinez gave up two runs while recording 11 outs. Ian Seymour picked up four outs. Griffin Jax came out of the bullpen to handle two innings. Then Cam Booser, Kevin Kelly and Bryan Baker finished the job in the eighth and ninth. “We knew what we were up against,” said Baker, who got the save in all three games. “To be able to come out and execute after a week off, it shows a lot about our group.” Meanwhile, two key role players delivered the biggest hits of the night for Tampa Bay. In the fourth inning of his postseason debut, Vilade dropped a home run just over the right-field fence for a solo homer off Max Fried. In the sixth, Victor Mesa Jr. blasted a tiebreaking, two-run shot to right-center and slowly backed out of the batter’s box as he stared into the Rays’ dugout.

“I love the energy we brought, man. We fought every single pitch on both sides of the ball from the very first pitch,” Martinez said. “Guys brought the energy every game, man. And when we do that, we're dangerous.” This was the Rays’ first postseason series win since the 2020 ALCS, when they beat the Astros in seven games. They didn’t advance in each of their past three trips to the playoffs, losing to the Red Sox in the 2021 ALDS before getting swept in AL Wild Card Series matchups against the Guardians (2022) and Rangers (‘23). But history could be on Tampa Bay’s side now. The Rays have only advanced past the ALDS twice before, in 2008 and ‘20, and they went to the World Series both times. Now, they are four wins away from their third Fall Classic appearance -- and eight away from the first championship in franchise history. Until then, the message won’t change. “The exact same,” Cash said. “Let's continue what we're doing.”
